places.name: Snell Arcade
places.summary: A 1928 arcade building on Central Avenue developed by C. Perry Snell and designed by Richard Kiehnel of Kiehnel and Elliott. It is on the National Register and is a city landmark.

heritage.architect: Richard Kiehnel and M. Leo Elliott (Kiehnel and Elliott)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: Landowner and developer C. Perry Snell built the arcade at 405 Central Avenue in 1928 to a design by Richard Kiehnel of the firm Kiehnel and Elliott. It is also known as the Rutland Building. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on November 4, 1982, and the city added it to its local register in 1986.
heritage.visiting: Seen from the sidewalk on the 400 block of Central Avenue downtown; it stands inside the Downtown St. Petersburg Historic District.

places.notes: No official site for the building was found (snellarcade.com redirects to an unrelated film site). Wikipedia's text says built 1928 while its category says 1926; NRIS gives 1928 as the significant year, used here. Local register year read from the city's register PDF (column order in the PDF makes the month uncertain, so only the year is given).

places.name: Open Air Post Office
places.summary: St. Petersburg's 1916–1917 post office at First Avenue North and Fourth Street, known as the Open Air Post Office. It is on the National Register and was among the first city landmarks, designated in 1986.

heritage.architect: George W. Stewart; M. C. Holliday (per NRIS)
heritage.style: Classical Revival with Spanish Colonial elements

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: The federal post office at the southwest corner of First Avenue North and Fourth Street North was built in 1916 and 1917 and is known as the Open Air Post Office. The National Park Service record names George W. Stewart and M. C. Holliday as its architects. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on April 4, 1975, and designated a city landmark in 1986.
heritage.visiting: On the southwest corner of First Avenue North and Fourth Street North, downtown.

places.notes: Whether it still operates as a USPS retail counter was not confirmed on a readable page (the USPS locator is script-rendered); the record claims only the building.

places.name: Detroit Hotel
places.summary: The building on the 200 block of Central Avenue that the city marks as the site of St. Petersburg's first hotel, the Detroit. It is a local historic landmark.

designations.name: St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: A bronze centennial plaque set in the Central Avenue sidewalk in 1988 says St. Petersburg's first hotel, the Detroit, was built on this site. The city's Demens Landing marker credits Peter Demens, who extended the Orange Belt railroad to St. Petersburg in 1888, with building the Detroit. The city added the Detroit Hotel at 201–215 Central Avenue to its local register in March 2010.
heritage.visiting: Seen from Central Avenue; look for the centennial plaque in the sidewalk on the north side of the 200 block.

places.notes: Source is the City of St. Petersburg's Markers and Monuments list (updated Sep 19, 2017) and the city's local register PDF. No built year is given because neither city page states one. The current use of the building (condominiums, shops) was not confirmed on a readable page. Geocoded to 215 Central Ave.

places.name: World's First Airline Monument
places.address: St. Pete Pier approach, 2nd Ave NE
places.summary: A stone monument with bronze plaques at the St. Pete Pier marking where the St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line began scheduled flights across Tampa Bay on January 1, 1914. The Pier map lists it in Benoist Centennial Plaza.

heritage.story: On January 1, 1914, the St. Petersburg–Tampa Airboat Line began what Wikipedia describes as the first scheduled airline service in the United States using a fixed-wing aircraft, with pilot Tony Jannus flying a Benoist airboat from St. Petersburg to Tampa in about 23 minutes. Former mayor Abram C. Pheil won the first round-trip ticket at auction with a bid of 400 dollars, and the service ran from January to May 1914. The city's markers list records two bronze plaques on a stone monument at the start of the pier approach on 2nd Avenue NE: one erected January 1, 1938, and one dedicated December 4, 1953, reading 'From this site, the St. Petersburg - Tampa Airboat Line, the world's first scheduled airline, began regular flights between St. Petersburg and Tampa, Jan. 1, 1914.' The St. Pete Pier now lists the spot as Benoist Centennial Plaza featuring the World's First Airline Monument.
heritage.visiting: On the St. Pete Pier approach (Pier map item 17). The St. Petersburg Museum of History, also in the Pier District, shows a working replica of the Benoist XIV airboat, per the Pier.

places.notes: The Pier's visit page and map legend (read Sep 27, 2026) name item 17 'Benoist Centennial Plaza featuring the World's First Airline Monument'. The city's markers list (updated 2017, before the new Pier opened) places the plaques on '2nd Avenue NE, s. side of the street, s. of Spa Beach'. No coordinates: neither geocoder has the plaza; the St. Petersburg Museum of History (OSM, 27.773968,-82.630552) is in the same Pier District but the exact plaza point was not confirmed. The city's history page says Jannus flew 'across Tampa Bay in 23 minutes'. Verifier (2026-09-27): re-read the Pier page, the markers PDF and Wikipedia. Completed the 1953 plaque quotation (it had been cut off) and corrected 'first ticket' to the first round-trip ticket. Still no coordinates: neither geocoder nor Nominatim knows the plaza or the monument.

places.name: Historic Old Northeast
places.summary: A residential historic district north of downtown St. Petersburg, listed in the National Register as the North Shore Historic District in 2003. It runs from 5th Avenue North to 30th Avenue North between 4th Street and Tampa Bay.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (North Shore Historic District)

heritage.story: The North Shore Historic District, commonly known as Old Northeast or Historic Old Northeast, is bounded by 4th Street North, 5th Avenue North, Tampa Bay and 30th Avenue North. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on February 20, 2003, with 2,975 historic buildings. The National Park Service record gives its periods of significance as 1900 to 1949 and its main styles as Bungalow/Craftsman and Colonial Revival.
heritage.visiting: Mostly homes, with some shops, restaurants, parks and city landmarks; walk or bike its streets north of downtown.

places.notes: The neighborhood association site (honna.org) is script-rendered; its home page only names the Historic Old Northeast Neighborhood Association. Point is the OSM neighbourhood node. Era set from the NRIS significant year 1910. Some blocks are also city local historic districts (North Shore sections, 2017–2018, per the city register PDF) but the PDF's column layout made the section names hard to pair with dates, so they are not listed as designations.

places.name: Roser Park Historic District
places.summary: An early 20th-century neighborhood on the hills along Booker Creek, south of downtown St. Petersburg, developed by Charles Roser. Its Historic Outdoor Museum is a route of 28 markers on the neighborhood's history.

heritage.style: Bungalow/Craftsman; Prairie School; Late 19th and 20th Century Revivals (NRIS)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
St. Petersburg local historic district

heritage.story: Charles Roser came to St. Petersburg in 1910 and broke ground on the Roser Park development in 1911. The city made Roser Park a local historic district in 1987, and it was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on April 1, 1998, with 146 historic buildings, bounded by 5th and 9th Streets South and 6th and 11th Avenues South. The neighborhood's Historic Outdoor Museum opened on April 25, 1999, first along Booker Creek from Fourth Street South to Martin Luther King Jr. Street South.
heritage.visiting: Walk the Historic Outdoor Museum: 28 markers on 3-foot wrought-iron poles describe homes and history. The association says (2025 update) it is restoring the markers with the St. Petersburg Museum of History.

places.quote: The plaques, mounted on 3-foot tall wrought-iron poles, describe historic homes, and some show early 20th-century views of the neighborhood
places.notes: Point is the OSM neighbourhood node for Roser Park. Wikipedia repeats a rumor that Roser invented the Fig Newton and notes Nabisco has no record of him; left out.

places.name: Historic Manhattan Casino
places.hours_text: Office Monday–Friday 9 am–4 pm; tours by appointment
places.summary: A 1925 dance hall on 22nd Street South that was the center of Black St. Petersburg's entertainment during segregation. Restored and reopened, it is rented for events and can be toured by appointment.
places.quote: Founded in 1925, the Manhattan Casino stands as a beacon of cultural significance in St. Petersburg’s history.

designations.name: St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: In 1925 African American entrepreneur Elder Jordan Sr. contracted with R. L. Sharpe to build a 12,000-square-foot, two-story entertainment hall on 22nd Street South; the city says it first opened as the Jordan Dance Hall in 1931 and later became the Manhattan Casino. It was part of 'The Deuces,' the business and entertainment hub of the African American community in segregation-era St. Pete, and a stop on the Chitlin' Circuit. Performers included Louis Armstrong, Duke Ellington, Count Basie, Cab Calloway, Ray Charles, Nat King Cole, Fats Domino and James Brown. It closed in 1968 and the city designated it a local landmark in 1994.
heritage.visiting: Tours by appointment through the venue; its Jordan Ballroom and Legacy Room are rented for events. It is a stop on the city's African American Heritage Trail.

places.notes: The official site (copyright City of St. Petersburg, contact manhattancasino@stpete.org) says 'after careful restoration, we're proud to reopen our doors' and 'tours are available by appointment'. The city's attractions page says 'Built in 1925' and 'first opened as the Jordan Dance Hall in 1931'; the heritage trail page says it was 'constructed in 1925 by Elder Jordan Sr. ... and his sons'. The city attractions page phone is 727-892-5496; the venue site's main number 727-892-5400 is used. Verifier (2026-09-27): historicmanhattancasino.org now redirects (301) to historicmanhattancasino.com (via http), so url and source_url point at the .com page, which was re-read: quote, tours by appointment, office hours, main phone and the two event rooms confirmed; it says no restaurant operates on site. The Chitlin' Circuit and 'Elder Jordan Sr. and his sons' are on the city's heritage-trail page. The Gabber's post list (read through its WordPress API) carries a Sep 9, 2026 headline 'St. Pete's Historic Manhattan Casino Reopens With Ribbon-Cutting'; the article body could not be read (bot check).

places.name: Weedon Island Preserve
places.price_text: Free admission to the preserve and the Cultural and Natural History Center; donations welcome
places.summary: A 3,000-acre county preserve on Tampa Bay in north St. Petersburg where Indigenous people lived for thousands of years. Its Cultural and Natural History Center has exhibits on that history, and the preserve says a 1,100-year-old dugout canoe from its shoreline can be seen in the Welcome Center.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Weeden Island Site)
St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: Indigenous peoples lived at the site for thousands of years; the preserve says their descendants developed the Weeden Island culture (an alternate spelling), which lasted some 800 years and is known for ceremonial pottery and burials with grave goods. The Weeden Island Site was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1972. In 2011 archaeologists and volunteers excavated a pine dugout canoe 39.9 feet long from the shoreline; radiocarbon dating placed it between AD 690 and 1010, and it is attributed to the Manasota culture. Later island history includes homesteaders, speakeasies, a Hollywood movie studio and a 1930s airport.
heritage.visiting: The Cultural and Natural History Center has exhibits, programs and tours; the preserve says the public can view the 1,100-year-old canoe in the Welcome Center. More than 4.7 miles of boardwalks and trails cross the preserve.

places.notes: Shared id with the outdoors slice (which owns the park record); this record adds the heritage block. The county page says the north paddling trail is closed at this time. The canoe page also says the canoe will be reassembled and displayed once conservation is complete; its first line says the public can now view it in the Welcome Center. Verifier (2026-09-27): summary reworded: the canoe page says the public can view the canoe 'in the Welcome Center' (and elsewhere that it will be displayed at the Center once conservation ends), so the summary no longer places it in the Center. The preserve's own site gives 3,195 acres; the county page gives 3,000.

places.name: African American Heritage Trail
aliases: St. Pete African American Heritage Trail
places.address: Starts at the Carter G. Woodson African American Museum, 2240 9th Ave S
places.summary: A self-guided walking tour of 19 markers in two corridors, 22nd Street South and 9th Avenue South, on the history of St. Petersburg's African American community. Both routes start at the Carter G. Woodson African American Museum.

heritage.story: The city says John and Anna Donaldson, the first African American settlers on the Pinellas peninsula, arrived in 1868. Under Jim Crow laws Black residents built their own commercial, professional and entertainment street along 22nd Street South; the 1931 City Charter set separate residential districts by race. The 22nd Street trail covers businesses, the Manhattan Casino, the 1948 Royal Theater and Mercy Hospital (opened 1923); the 9th Avenue trail covers churches, Jordan Elementary School, the Fannye Ayer Ponder Council House and the Jordan Park housing complex, which opened in 1941 with 446 apartments.
heritage.visiting: Each corridor is about 1.25 miles with ten stops. Groups and classes can arrange a guided walking or trolley tour through the African American Heritage Association, per the city.

places.notes: Point is the trail start (Woodson museum, 2240 9th Ave S). The heritage trail's own site (afamheritagestpete.com) did not respond (connection reset / HTTP 503) on Sep 27, 2026. The city page says 'nineteen markers' and also 'ten trail stops' per corridor; both are reported as the city states them.

places.name: Gulfport Casino Ballroom
places.summary: Gulfport's waterfront casino ballroom on Boca Ciega Bay, first built in 1906 at the end of a dock and rebuilt in the 1930s. It is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Gulfport Casino)

heritage.story: The first casino was built in 1906 at the end of the dock into Boca Ciega Bay as a station and ticket office, with a post office and a refreshment stand. The current building dates from a reconstruction in the 1930s. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on August 8, 2014. The Gulfport Merchants Chamber calls it the original casino ballroom that still hosts swing dances.
heritage.visiting: On Shore Boulevard at the foot of Beach Boulevard on the Gulfport waterfront.

places.name: Jungle Prada Site
places.address: Park Street North at Elbow Lane
places.summary: An archaeological site on Boca Ciega Bay with remains of Tocobaga mounds, partly inside a small city park. It is also identified as the landing place of the Narváez expedition.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: The Tocobaga inhabited the site for about 600 years, from roughly 1000 to 1600 CE, in a village complex whose mounds once stretched more than 3 miles along Boca Ciega Bay; most were removed for fill during 20th-century development. The remaining mounds include a 12-foot plaza mound and a long midden mound running from the city park onto private property. The site is identified with the landing of the Narváez expedition, and the Diocese of St. Petersburg placed a marker there for what it calls the first Catholic Mass in Florida. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on February 4, 2003.
heritage.visiting: The public part is the city's Jungle Prada de Narvaez park, with picnic tables, a fishing pier and a boat launch; the better-preserved mounds are on private land.

places.notes: No city page for Jungle Prada park was found; facts are from Wikipedia and the NPS NRIS record. Wikipedia says the private mounds and a small museum are 'accessible by guided tour'; not repeated because no current tour page was found. Point is the OSM park (leisure=park 'Jungle Prada').

places.name: Historic Kenwood
places.summary: A National Register district of bungalows just north of St. Petersburg's Grand Central District, developed from 1912. The neighborhood association calls it St. Pete's first suburb.

heritage.style: Bungalow/Craftsman (NRIS); frame and masonry vernacular, Tudor, Mediterranean and Colonial Revival also present

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Kenwood Historic District)

heritage.story: In 1912 Philadelphia developer Charles Hall bought 160 acres of avocado groves about two miles northwest of downtown and began selling building lots; his first model home, built in 1918, is now the Craftsman House Gallery. Most homes were built between the 1920s and the 1950s, and 170 were moved here from other neighborhoods in the 1930s. The district, with 2,203 historic buildings, was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2003; St. Petersburg High School (1926) stands in it on 5th Avenue North. Wikipedia notes that urban pioneers began reviving Kenwood and the Grand Central District in the early 1990s and that the LGBT community played a notable role in the revitalization.
heritage.visiting: A residential neighborhood; walk its brick avenues and hexagon-paver sidewalks among bungalows. Several sections are also city local historic districts.

places.quote: Kenwood was St. Pete’s first suburb and its first neighborhood for year-round residents
places.notes: Wikipedia says homes were built 1912–1945; the association says 1920s–1950s; the association wording is used. Point is the OSM neighbourhood node. Verifier (2026-09-27): added the lgbtq topic and one sentence from Wikipedia's article (read), which also confirms the brick avenues and hexagonal paver sidewalks.

places.name: Downtown St. Petersburg Historic District
places.summary: The National Register district covering much of downtown St. Petersburg between 5th Avenue North, Beach Drive, Central Avenue and 9th Street, with 367 historic buildings. Many carry bronze plaques that mark them as part of the district.

heritage.style: Late Victorian; Late 19th and 20th Century Revivals (NRIS)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: The district was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on April 30, 2004, and is bounded by 5th Avenue North, Beach Drive NE, Central Avenue and 9th Street North. It contains 367 historic buildings and 7 objects, including the Snell Arcade, the Coliseum, the Princess Martha Hotel and First United Methodist Church. The National Park Service record gives 1888 as its significant year and lists architecture, community planning, commerce and entertainment as its areas of significance; the city's Demens Landing marker says Peter Demens extended the Orange Belt railroad to St. Petersburg that year.
heritage.visiting: Walk Central Avenue and the streets around Williams Park. Buildings in the district carry bronze 'contributing structure' plaques (awarded in 2004), and small 1988 centennial plaques set in the sidewalks mark vanished landmarks.

places.notes: Point is Williams Park (330 2nd Ave N), a representative spot inside the district. 'the year the railroad arrived': the city's Demens Landing marker (markers PDF) says Demens extended the Orange Belt railroad to St. Petersburg in 1888; verifier may drop the clause if the pairing is judged editorial. Verifier (2026-09-27): reworded the 1888 sentence so the railroad fact is attributed to the city's Demens Landing marker rather than presented as the NPS's reason.

places.name: Mirror Lake Community Library
places.summary: St. Petersburg's Carnegie library, opened on Mirror Lake in 1915 and still a branch of the city library system. It is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (St. Petersburg Public Library)
St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: The city won a 17,500 dollar grant from the Carnegie Corporation in 1913 and in 1914 chose a site on the banks of the city reservoir, now Mirror Lake. The Beaux-Arts library by Henry D. Whitfield opened in December 1915; the city calls it St. Petersburg's first library. The city refused Black residents access when it opened and began admitting them to the basement in 1944. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1986.
heritage.visiting: A working city library branch; the city says it remains in operation today.

places.notes: Library hours not captured (the locations page lists address and phone only). NRIS spells the architect 'Whitefield, Henry'; Wikipedia gives Henry D. Whitfield, used here. is_free: public library (no admission). Verifier (2026-09-27): 'first permanent home of the city's public library' was not on a page read; replaced with the city history page's 'the city's first library'.

places.name: Huggins-Stengel Field
places.summary: A baseball field in Crescent Lake Park built in 1925 for New York Yankees spring training and later used by the Mets and Orioles. It is on the National Register and is a city landmark.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
St. Petersburg Register of Historic Places (local landmark)

heritage.story: The field in Crescent Lake Park was built in 1925 as the New York Yankees' spring training practice field under manager Miller Huggins, and was renamed Miller Huggins Field in 1931. Babe Ruth, Lou Gehrig and Joe DiMaggio trained here, and later Casey Stengel's Yankees; after Stengel took over the new New York Mets, the Mets trained here and the field was renamed Huggins-Stengel Field in 1963. The Baltimore Orioles used it from 1992 to 1995. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2019.
heritage.visiting: In Crescent Lake Park; two bronze plaques honor Miller Huggins and Casey Stengel. The field now hosts high school and college games, per Wikipedia.

places.notes: No city parks page for the field was found (stpeteparksrec.org pages are script-rendered). The NRHP list gives the listing date Aug 27, 2019.

places.name: Pass-a-Grille Historic District
places.summary: The old beach town at the southern tip of St. Pete Beach, listed in the National Register in 1989 and expanded in 2003. The city publishes a self-guided walking tour of 21 of its historic buildings.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
National Register of Historic Places (Pass-a-Grille Historic District boundary increase)

heritage.story: Zephaniah Phillips, Pass-a-Grille's first homesteader, claimed 79 acres here in 1886; the city's tour says the house at 101 Eighth Avenue incorporates part of his cabin. Residents voted to incorporate at a town meeting on February 2, 1911, and in 1957 Pass-a-Grille was consolidated with Don CeSar, Belle Vista and St. Petersburg Beach into the City of St. Petersburg Beach. The Pass-a-Grille Community Church was dedicated on Christmas Day 1917; its later owner, Joan Haley, left it to Pinellas County in 1989 for a museum of the barrier islands. The district was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on October 19, 1989, with 97 historic buildings, and expanded in 2003.
heritage.visiting: Follow the city's self-guided walking tour (an online story map of 21 buildings). Eighth Avenue keeps early commercial buildings such as the 1912 Merry store at 107 Eighth Avenue.

places.notes: The tour (City of St. Pete Beach, compiled by Barbara Baker Smith, historian of the Pass-a-Grille Community Church) was read through the ArcGIS item data API (arcgis.com/sharing/rest/content/items/fc43a93a44c64a0e8047b4c2cb9280e8/data). Point is 107 8th Ave, a building on the tour. The former church is the Gulf Beaches Historical Museum per Wikipedia; its own site (gulfbeachesmuseum.org) returned a bot check, so the museum has no record here and its hours/status are unconfirmed. Verifier (2026-09-27): story map re-read through the ArcGIS item-data API: Phillips homestead (79 acres, 1886), the Feb 2, 1911 town meeting, the church dedicated Christmas Day 1917, Joan Haley's 1989 bequest, the 1912 store at 107 Eighth Avenue and the 21-building tour all confirmed; the 1957 consolidation is on the city's Community History page. Added the 2003 boundary increase (ref 03000943) from Wikipedia's infobox.

places.name: Fort De Soto Batteries
places.address: Fort De Soto Park, Mullet Key
places.price_text: County parking fee of 6 dollars to enter the park
places.summary: The Spanish–American War coastal fort on Mullet Key that gave Fort De Soto Park its name, with its 12-inch mortar battery, brick roads and a small museum. The battery is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Fort Desoto Batteries)

heritage.story: Mullet Key was declared a military reservation in 1849 after an Army engineers' survey. Construction of Fort De Soto, a subpost of Fort Dade on Egmont Key, began in November 1898 and was completed in 1906; Battery Laidley held eight 12-inch coast defense mortars and Battery Bigelow two 3-inch guns, to protect Tampa Bay, and the fort was active until 1910. Pinellas County bought the land in 1938, sold it back to the federal government in 1941 for a World War II gunnery and bombing range, and repurchased it in 1948. The 12-inch mortar battery was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1977.
heritage.visiting: Inside Fort De Soto Park: the battery with its remaining 12-inch mortars, two British rapid-fire rifles of 1890 vintage installed in 1982, markers where the post's buildings stood, and the Quartermaster Storehouse Museum. A 6.8-mile paved trail links the campground and beaches to the fort.

places.notes: Separate record for the fort inside the outdoors slice's fort-de-soto-park. Point is the OSM building 'Battery Laidly, Original Brick Road 1898'. The county page gives the 6 dollar parking fee (plus a 0.35 dollar app/text convenience fee). Verifier (2026-09-27): corrected the batteries: Wikipedia gives Battery Laidley eight 12-inch mortars and Battery Bigelow two 3-inch guns (the old text gave both batteries mortars). County page re-read: 6-dollar parking, 7 a.m. to sunset, 1938/1941/1948 dates, the 1890 British rifles (installed March 1982) and the Quartermaster Storehouse Museum confirmed. The outdoors verifier logged the county's current park closures (Bay Pier end, repaving) on fort-de-soto-park.

places.name: Egmont Key State Park
places.summary: An island at the mouth of Tampa Bay, reached only by boat, with the 1858 Egmont Key Lighthouse and the ruins of Fort Dade. It is a state park and national wildlife refuge.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Egmont Key)

heritage.story: The lighthouse that stands today replaced an earlier light in 1858 and is maintained by the U.S. Coast Guard. At the end of the Third Seminole War the island held a camp for captured Seminoles, and Union forces occupied it during the Civil War. Fort Dade was built in 1898 for the Spanish–American War and housed 300 residents; Egmont Key stayed a military reservation until 1923. The Egmont Key Alliance says the island has lost more than half its land since 1898 to storms and rising seas, and that in 2024 Hurricanes Helene and Milton pushed surge 15 feet up the lighthouse and closed the island for more than six months.
heritage.visiting: Reached only by boat; ferries run from Fort De Soto. Since August 2026 the state park says all structures remain closed to the public, so the lighthouse and the Fort Dade ruins are seen from outside; the south end and part of the east beach are closed year-round for nesting birds.

places.notes: Shared id with the outdoors slice (which owns the park record and checked the ferry). floridastateparks.org returned HTTP 403 to WebFetch and bot-checks curl. 'Walk the Fort Dade ruins, batteries and brick roads' rests on the Alliance's note that volunteers 'helped restore brick trails, lighthouse surroundings, and Fort Dade structures' and on Wikipedia; the outdoors record states it directly. Status open: the Alliance describes the post-2024 closure in the past tense. Verifier (2026-09-27): the state park page was read in full through the r.jina.ai reader (floridastateparks.org blocks curl and WebFetch). It carries an alert effective Aug. 12, 2026: park open, all structures closed to the public; hours 8 a.m. to sunset; no fee. Coordinates changed to the lighthouse GPS point the park publishes (N 27 36.047 W 82 45.634); the old OSM point was about 800 m south. egmontkey.info now redirects to egmontkey.org, whose timeline confirms the 15-foot surge, the 6+ month closure and 'over half its landmass since 1898'.
places.hours_text: 8 a.m. to sunset
places.price_text: No park fee (reached only by boat)
places.status_note: Open. The state park's alert effective Aug. 12, 2026 says the park is open but all structures remain closed to the public. The Egmont Key Alliance says the island was closed for more than six months after Hurricanes Helene and Milton in 2024.

places.name: Old Pinellas County Courthouse
places.summary: Pinellas County's Classical Revival courthouse in downtown Clearwater, designed by Francis J. Kennard, with its 1917 building and 1920s additions. It is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Pinellas County Courthouse, Old)

heritage.story: Designed by Francis J. Kennard, the courthouse replaced a hastily built structure that had been put up to help establish Clearwater as the county seat. The National Park Service record lists 1917, 1924 and 1926 as its significant years, for the original building and its additions. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on June 25, 1992.
heritage.visiting: Seen from Court Street in downtown Clearwater.

places.notes: Wikipedia's text says 'constructed in 1918' while its infobox and NRIS give 1917, 1924, 1926; NRIS used. Current use of the building (county offices) not confirmed on a county page; the record claims only the exterior.

places.name: Harbor Oaks Residential District
places.summary: An early 20th-century residential district on Clearwater Harbor just south of downtown Clearwater, developed by Dean Alvord. It is on the National Register.

heritage.style: Colonial Revival; Late 19th and 20th Century Revivals; Prairie School (NRIS)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Developer Dean Alvord built Harbor Oaks in the early 20th century. Its residents included Brooklyn Dodgers owner Charles Ebbets, writer Rex Beach and engineer Donald Roebling, whose estate at 700 Orange Avenue is also separately listed in the National Register. Bounded by Druid Road, South Fort Harrison Avenue, Lotus Path and Clearwater Harbor, the district has 81 historic buildings and was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on March 15, 1988.
heritage.visiting: A residential neighborhood; the homes are seen from the street.

places.notes: Point is the Donald Roebling Estate (700 Orange Ave), which Wikipedia lists as a notable property in the district. No City of Clearwater page on the district was read. Verifier (2026-09-27): confirmed the Donald Roebling Estate (700 Orange Avenue) is separately listed (NRHP 79000689, 1979) on Wikipedia's Pinellas NRHP list; its listed point (27.9575, -82.8047) matches the record's.

places.name: Andrews Memorial Chapel
places.summary: An 1888 Carpenter Gothic church built by Dunedin's pioneer families, saved and moved to Hammock Park by the Dunedin Historical Society. The Dunedin History Museum runs it for weddings and community events.
places.quote: Historic Andrews Memorial Chapel was built by Dunedin’s Pioneer families in 1888 and rescued from demolition by the Dunedin Historical Society in 1970.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Built in 1888 as Andrews Memorial Church at Scotland Street and Highland Avenue, the building was renamed Andrews Memorial Chapel and moved in 1926 to make way for what is now the First Presbyterian Church of Dunedin. The Dunedin Historical Society bought it in 1970 to save it from demolition, cut it in half and moved it to Hammock Park, where restoration began in 1974. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on July 31, 1972.
heritage.visiting: Next to Hammock Park. The Dunedin History Museum operates the chapel for weddings, christenings, memorials and community events; contact the chapel manager for access.

places.notes: Wikipedia says it is open for visits on Sundays from 2 to 4 PM; the museum's page does not say so, so no public hours are given. Verifier (2026-09-27): coordinates moved about 100 m to the OSM chapel building (place_of_worship node on Buena Vista Drive); the Census point was on the San Mateo Drive centerline.

places.name: Tarpon Springs Sponge Docks
places.summary: The Anclote River waterfront along Dodecanese Boulevard where Greek divers built Tarpon Springs' sponge industry. It is the core of the Greektown Historic District, with the 1907 Sponge Exchange, sponge boats, shops and Greek restaurants.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Tarpon Springs Sponge Exchange)
National Register of Historic Places (Tarpon Springs Greektown Historic District, a Traditional Cultural Property)

heritage.story: After Tarpon Springs was incorporated in 1887, John Cheney, a promoter associated with Hamilton Disston, began harvesting sponges from the Gulf, and by 1890 the industry was established. Experienced divers from Greece followed, using rubberized suits and helmets; by 1905 more than 500 Greek sponge divers worked from 50 boats. Sponge buyers built the Sponge Exchange in 1907, a courtyard building where catches were stored for twice-weekly auctions. The Greektown Historic District, about 140 acres around the docks, was listed in 2014 as the first Traditional Cultural Property in Florida.
heritage.visiting: Walk Dodecanese Boulevard past docked sponge boats, sponge shops, Greek restaurants and bakeries; the Sponge Exchange now holds more than 30 shops and restaurants, and SpongeDocks.net says sponge auctions are held weekly.

places.notes: Shared id with see-pinellas (which owns the place record); this record adds the heritage block. The Sponge Exchange's NRHP ref 72000348 (listed 1972) comes from Wikipedia's Pinellas NRHP list; its NPGallery page returned no metadata. Four sponge boats (Duchess, George N. Cretekos, N. K. Symi, St. Nicholas III and VI) are also separately listed (1990) per the same list. SpongeDocks.net says 'For 30 years, the sponge industry was the largest industry in Florida'; not repeated as fact. Point is the OSM 'The Sponge Exchange' (see-pinellas uses 28.155818,-82.762023).

places.name: St. Nicholas Greek Orthodox Cathedral
places.hours_text: Typically open for prayer on weekdays 9:00 a.m.–3:00 p.m., subject to services
places.summary: The domed 1943 cathedral of Tarpon Springs' Greek Orthodox parish, paid for in part by sponge divers' harvests. It leads the city's Epiphany celebration each January 6.
places.quote: When the need for a larger building arose, the sponge divers funded the new cathedral by donating a portion of each sponge harvest to St. Nicholas.

heritage.story: Greek immigrants built the parish's first church, a frame building, in 1907 and named it for Saint Nicholas, protector of seafaring people. The current cathedral was completed in 1943; its marble from Mount Penteli, a gift of the Greek government, had first been shipped to New York for the 1939 World's Fair. The church was elevated to a cathedral in January 1979. Each January 6 the parish holds its Epiphany celebration, when young men dive into Spring Bayou to retrieve a cross.
heritage.visiting: Visitors are welcome; the cathedral is typically open for prayer on weekdays from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m. Public parking lots are a block away.

places.notes: Architect (Eugene Brothers of Chicago), 'Neo-Byzantine' and the Epiphany description are from Wikipedia; the rest from the cathedral's pages. The parish's page says services are in Greek and English and asks for modest dress.

places.name: Tarpon Springs Historic District
places.summary: The late 19th-century resort town around Spring Bayou in Tarpon Springs, with 145 historic buildings. It is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: A. W. Ormond and his daughter Mary built a cabin near Spring Bayou in 1876, and Mary Ormond named the settlement Tarpon Springs in 1879. Hamilton Disston's 1880 purchase of four million acres of Florida's west coast included the town, which Disston's investment turned into a winter resort for wealthy Northerners; it was incorporated in 1887 with 52 residents. The district around Spring Bayou, bounded by Read, Hibiscus, Orange and Lemon Streets and Levis Avenue, has 145 historic buildings and was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on December 6, 1990.
heritage.visiting: Walk the winding streets around Spring Bayou; the Safford House Museum is in the district.

places.notes: Point is the Safford House (23 Parkin Ct), which Tarpon Arts says is in the historic district. SpongeDocks.net notes the fish Mary Ormond saw were actually mullet, not tarpon.

places.name: Safford House Museum
places.hours_text: Wednesday–Friday 11 AM–3 PM; docent tours start 11:15 AM, 12:15, 1:15 and 2:15 PM
places.price_text: Adults 5 dollars; Tarpon Springs residents 3 dollars (ID required)
places.parking_text: Free lot next to the house
places.summary: The 1883 home of Anson P. K. Safford, a former Arizona territorial governor and early developer of Tarpon Springs, restored and run by the city as a Victorian house museum with docent tours.
places.quote: Visiting the home of one of the city’s original developers is a journey back in time.

heritage.style: Late Victorian (NRIS); Florida vernacular (per Tarpon Arts)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: The house was home to Anson P. K. Safford, former territorial governor of Arizona and one of Tarpon Springs' original developers, his wife Soledad, and his sister Dr. Mary Jane Safford, the town's first doctor. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1974 and donated to the city in 1994; restoration was funded by the state Division of Historical Resources and the city, and it is furnished with period pieces and original family possessions.
heritage.visiting: Docent-led tours of about 40 minutes, Wednesday to Friday; arrive 15 to 20 minutes early for a short video on the Safford family.

places.notes: Tarpon Arts is the City of Tarpon Springs' cultural and civic services arm (the city site links to it). Era 'frontier' because the house dates from 1883 (the era table ends frontier at 1883).

places.name: Unitarian Universalist Church of Tarpon Springs
places.hours_text: Sunday services 10:30 a.m.; tours of the Inness paintings by appointment
places.summary: A 1908 church at Grand Boulevard and Read Street in Tarpon Springs that displays paintings George Inness Jr. created for it; the church says it holds the largest public collection of his paintings anywhere. The paintings can be seen by appointment.
places.quote: Come experience the largest single collection of the beautiful paintings George Inness Jr. created for our Church; now displayed in our recently restored sanctuary.

heritage.story: Fourteen Universalists formed a congregation in Tarpon Springs in 1885 on land donated by Anson P. K. Safford. After fire destroyed its first building, the present church was built in 1908 at Grand Boulevard and Read Street. When a tropical storm broke sanctuary windows on September 28, 1918, George Inness Jr. and his family donated paintings to fill the openings, the start of the church's Inness collection. Sinkhole damage closed the buildings late in 2013; after nearly six years of work the church was rededicated on September 29, 2019.
heritage.visiting: Call or email the church to schedule a tour of the paintings; Sunday services are at 10:30 a.m.

places.notes: 'Largest public collection' is the church's own claim ('the largest public collection of George Inness, Jr.'s paintings anywhere'). No NRHP designation of its own was found (it may be a contributing building of the Tarpon Springs Historic District; not verified). Verifier (2026-09-27): summary now attributes 'largest public collection' to the church and drops 'on Spring Bayou' (the church page places Spring Bayou in its local history, not at the church). Coordinates moved about 60 m to the OSM church node.

places.name: Anclote Key Lighthouse
places.summary: An 1887 cast-iron skeletal lighthouse on the southern end of Anclote Key, three miles off Tarpon Springs, relit in 2003 inside Anclote Key Preserve State Park. Volunteers open it for climbing on monthly open-house weekends from October to May; the island is reached only by boat.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Anclote Keys Light)

heritage.story: The lighthouse was built in 1887 on Anclote Key, the largest of the Anclote Keys. After it was automated in 1952 the tower and other buildings were often vandalized, and the Coast Guard deactivated the light in 1984; the site passed to the State of Florida and became part of Anclote Key Preserve State Park. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1999 and, by 2003, had been restored and relit with a reproduction fourth-order Fresnel lens.
heritage.visiting: Reached only by private boat or ferry: the state park lists Island Paradise Charters and Parrotdise Express, and Odyssey Cruises from the Sponge Docks. The Friends of Anclote Key open the tower for climbing the second weekend of each month, October to May, and run private tours; on other days the tower is seen from its locked fence.

places.notes: floridastateparks.org blocks both tools (HTTP 403), so whether the tower can be climbed or toured is not stated; the outdoors slice owns anclote-key-preserve-state-park. Point is the OSM lighthouse node. The Visit St. Pete/Clearwater article (HTTP 403 to curl) was dropped as a source.

places.name: 1914 Plant City High School Community Center
places.summary: Plant City's original 1914 high school building on North Collins Street, now a community center. It is on the National Register.

heritage.architect: Willis R. Biggers (NRIS also lists Dudley and Carlton)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Plant City High School)

heritage.story: Tampa architect Willis R. Biggers designed the original Plant City High School, built in 1914 at 605 North Collins Street. The high school later moved to a new building completed in 1972, and the 1914 building became a community center. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on February 4, 1981.
heritage.visiting: A community center on North Collins Street; the city history page says the East Hillsborough Historical Society is on its first floor.

places.name: Bing Rooming House Museum
places.summary: A boarding house built about 1928 in Plant City, run by Janie Wheeler Bing for African American travelers barred from segregated hotels; now an African American history museum. It is on the National Register and is closed for hurricane repairs.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: The house was built about 1928 as a boarding house and was operated by Janie Wheeler Bing for African Americans who were not allowed to stay in segregated white hotels or eat in white restaurants. The National Park Service lists its area of significance as Black heritage, with periods from 1925 to 1974. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on September 14, 2002, and has since been renovated as a museum.
heritage.visiting: Closed for repairs after Hurricane Milton; the museum offers limited private tours by phone and says it presents Plant City African American history from an African American perspective.

places.notes: Shared id with around-daytrips (its verifier also found the closure). Status from plantcitybinghouse.com read Sep 27, 2026: THE MUSEUM IS CLOSED THRU DECEMBER 2025 plus a fundraising total as of December 1, 2025; no reopening date is given, so the record stays temporarily-closed. places.name: Historic Pasco County Courthouse
places.summary: Pasco County's 1909 courthouse in downtown Dade City, designed by Edward Columbus Hosford. It is on the National Register and the city's historic register.

heritage.architect: Edward Columbus Hosford (built by the Mutual Construction Company)
heritage.style: Classical Revival (NRIS; Wikipedia describes it as Beaux-Arts)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places
Dade City Historic Register (Old Pasco County Courthouse and Bandstand)

heritage.story: Georgia architect Edward Columbus Hosford designed the courthouse, which the Mutual Construction Company built in 1909 on Meridian Avenue; the National Park Service record gives 1909 and 1920 as its significant years. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on September 20, 2006, and Dade City's municipal historic register includes the old courthouse and its bandstand. In recent years the county clerk has held free Valentine's Day weddings on its steps.
heritage.visiting: In downtown Dade City at 37918 Meridian Avenue; seen from the street.

places.name: Saint Leo Abbey
places.summary: A Benedictine monastery founded in 1889 beside what is now Saint Leo University, with the Romanesque Church of the Holy Cross, consecrated in 1948. Its historic district is on the National Register.

heritage.architect: Frank Parziole (Church of the Holy Cross)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (St. Leo Abbey Historic District)

heritage.story: Judge Edmund F. Dunne founded the Catholic Colony of San Antonio in 1882, and Father Gerard Pilz arrived in 1886 as the first Benedictine in Florida. On June 4, 1889, Saint Leo College (now Saint Leo University) and the Benedictine mission that became Saint Leo Abbey were founded on land Dunne conveyed to the order; it was raised to an abbey on September 25, 1902. Abbot Francis Sadlier commissioned the Church of the Holy Cross in 1935; designed by Tampa architect Frank Parziole, it was consecrated on January 29, 1948. The abbey's historic district was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1998.

places.notes: The abbey's own site (saintleoabbey.org) returned HTTP 403 to both curl and WebFetch, so visiting hours, Mass times and retreat-house details are not given. NRIS names Bro. Anthony Poiger as an architect and gives 1912, 1936 and 1941 as significant years for the district. Address is the NRIS address (33701 FL 52); coordinates from Wikipedia. Verifier (2026-09-27): saintleoabbey.org still returns 403 (Cloudflare) to curl, WebFetch and r.jina.ai. Church dates changed to 1936–1948 (Wikipedia: commissioned 1935, groundbreaking September 19, 1936, consecrated January 29, 1948). places.name: Temple Terrace Golf and Country Club
places.summary: The 1922 golf course around which Temple Terrace was built as one of the country's early golf communities, on land that was Bertha Palmer's hunting preserve. The course is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Temple Terrace Golf Course)

heritage.story: Chicago businesswoman Bertha Palmer bought the land early in the 1900s as a hunting preserve; after her death in 1918 investors formed two companies to build a golf course and homes and a 5,000-acre orange grove, which the city says was the largest in the world in the 1920s. Tom Bendelow's course opened in 1922 with a clubhouse by M. Leo Elliott, three years before the city was incorporated; the clubhouse became part of Florida College in the 1930s, and the course hosted the first Florida Open in 1925. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 2012. The city calls Temple Terrace one of the first golfing communities in the United States and adopted a local historic preservation program in 2023.
heritage.visiting: The course and club are on Inverness Avenue in Temple Terrace; Riverhills Drive along the Hillsborough River dates from 1921.

places.notes: Chosen as the Temple Terrace heritage record because it is the city's only NRHP listing and the core of its 1920s golf-community plan. Wikipedia's Temple Terrace article describes Mediterranean Revival villas, but that section is tagged unreferenced, so 'Mediterranean Revival' is not claimed. Whether the course is open to non-members was not confirmed (no club page read); the record does not say it is public. The city's History Map page reset the connection. places.name: El Retiro
aliases: El Retiro at Bok Tower Gardens

places.summary: A 20-room Mediterranean-style winter house built in the early 1930s for Bethlehem Steel executive Charles Austin Buck, with gardens by the Olmsted firm, inside Bok Tower Gardens. It is on the National Register and is seen on docent-led tours.

heritage.architect: Charles R. Wait (house); William Lyman Phillips of the Olmsted firm (gardens)

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: Charles Austin Buck, a Bethlehem Steel vice president, hired the Olmsted firm to design his winter estate next to Mountain Lake; William Lyman Phillips began the gardens in 1929, and architect Charles Wait was engaged in 1930 to design the 12,900-square-foot house with barrel-tile roofs, carved doors and wrought iron. The family used it six to twelve weeks a year. In 1970 an effort led by Nellie Lee Holt Bok, daughter-in-law of Edward W. Bok, brought the home into Bok Tower Gardens, and landscape architect Rudy Favretti restored it with volunteers. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1985.
heritage.visiting: Buy the tour at the Entrance Gate or Visitor Center before walking to the house. Stairs lead to the second floor and there is no elevator; food and drink are not allowed inside.

places.notes: Id chosen to avoid a clash with any other 'el-retiro'. The admission page also offers a combined garden plus El Retiro tour at 35 dollars per adult and 17 dollars ages 6–17. Built years: gardens begun 1929, architect hired 1930, NRIS significant years 1930 and 1932; Wikipedia says work was completed 1929–1930; '1929–1932' spans the sources. Point is the OSM feature 'El Retiro' (historic=heritage); Wikipedia's coordinate is about 1 km east. Verifier (2026-09-27): added the seasonal tour hours from the El Retiro page; 'built about 1930' changed to the page's 'early 1930s'. Prices, the 25-dollar garden admission from Oct 1 and the tour rules re-confirmed.

places.address: Between Lemon Street and Lake Mirror Drive
places.summary: A 1920s Classical Revival promenade and civic center on the shore of Lake Mirror in downtown Lakeland, designed by Charles Wellford Leavitt. It is on the National Register.

heritage.architect: Charles Wellford Leavitt (designer); H. B. Trauger

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Lake Mirror Promenade)

heritage.story: The promenade, also called the First Civic Center, was built in two phases and completed in 1928 to a design by Charles Wellford Leavitt of New York. In 1946 the city of Lakeland dedicated it to Lakeland native Frances Langford for her work with the USO and her singing and acting career, and it was rededicated with a new marker in 2013. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on January 27, 1983.
heritage.visiting: A lakefront promenade on Lake Mirror in downtown Lakeland, between Lemon Street and Lake Mirror Drive.

places.name: Braden Castle Park Historic District
places.summary: A small Bradenton neighborhood at the meeting of the Manatee and Braden rivers that holds the tabby ruins of Joseph Braden's 1850 house. It is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places

heritage.story: The district contains the ruins of the 1850 Braden House, a tabby house owned by Joseph Braden. The National Park Service record gives 1850 and 1924 as its significant years. Bounded by the Manatee and Braden rivers, Ponce de Leon Street and Pelot Avenue, the district has 192 historic buildings and 3 structures and was listed in the National Register of Historic Places on May 9, 1983.
heritage.visiting: The Bradenton Area Convention and Visitors Bureau lists Braden Castle at 45 Braden Castle Drive as a historical attraction; the district around it is a residential neighborhood.

places.name: Palmetto Historical Park
places.hours_text: Carnegie Library open Tuesday–Friday and the 1st and 3rd Saturdays, 10 am–12 pm and 1–4 pm; free guided tours of the other buildings at 11 am
places.parking_text: Street parking, and a lot behind the buildings at 1037 6th St W
places.summary: A county-run history park on Palmetto's Old Main Street with the 1914 Carnegie Library, an 1880 post office, a schoolhouse, a cottage museum, a military museum and a replica chapel. Admission and guided tours are free.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Palmetto Historic District)

heritage.story: In 1982 a group led by Josephine Harrison organized to save Palmetto's original post office, built about 1880 for postmaster Mary Nettles, and moved it to the corner of 10th Avenue and 6th Street West, the former site of the town's first city hall and school; it was dedicated as Heritage Station in 1983. Andrew Carnegie contributed 10,000 dollars toward the 1914 Carnegie Library, which later served as town hall and school library and now holds the local history archives. A 1984 survey led to the listing of the surrounding Palmetto Historic District in the National Register in 1986.
heritage.visiting: Start upstairs in the Carnegie Library; the other buildings are kept locked and are seen on the free 11 am guided tour. The Manatee County Agricultural Museum is also in the park.

places.notes: Run under an interlocal agreement involving the Manatee County Clerk's Historical Resources Department. The tours page gives two schedules: 'Tuesdays, Fridays & the 1st and 3rd Saturdays of the month at 11:00 AM due to school programming' (Sept–May) and '11:00 AM every day that the park is open'. The park's story page says the district was listed Dec 30, 1986; NRIS gives Nov 6, 1986; only the year is used. Shared id with around-daytrips (added by its verifier the same day).

places.name: 1860 Manatee County Courthouse
places.address: Manatee Village Historical Park, 1404 Manatee Ave E
places.summary: Manatee County's first courthouse, a small wood-frame building from 1860, now one of the historic buildings at Manatee Village Historical Park. It is on the National Register.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Manatee County Courthouse, Original)

heritage.story: Manatee County was formed in 1855, and five years later the community built this small wood-framed courthouse; all government business for the county's 5,000 square miles took place in its courtroom. The building later belonged to the Manatee United Methodist congregation, and when it and the congregation's 1887 church were slated for demolition in 1974, the Manatee County Historical Commission moved both to the new museum in December 1975. It was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1976.
heritage.visiting: Seen at Manatee Village Historical Park, open Monday–Friday and the 2nd and 4th Saturdays, 9 AM–4 PM; admission is free.

places.notes: Separate record for the NRHP-listed 1860 courthouse inside around-daytrips' manatee-village-historical-park (whose record lists no designations); could instead be merged into it as a designation. Hours and admission read from manateevillage.org (via WebFetch). Verifier (2026-09-27): name changed to '1860 Manatee County Courthouse' (Manatee Village calls it the 1860 Courthouse; NRIS 'Manatee County Courthouse, Original') so it is not confused with the 1913 courthouse downtown; the old name is kept as an alias. Every claim re-checked on manateevillage.org.

places.name: Fort Cooper State Park
places.price_text: 3 dollars per vehicle (honor box; correct change required)
places.summary: A 700-acre state park near Inverness on the site of a Second Seminole War outpost, with a reconstructed palisade, Lake Holathlikaha and nearly five miles of self-guided trails. A battle reenactment is held each March, per Citrus County's tourism office.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Fort Cooper)

heritage.story: During the Second Seminole War the U.S. Army set up a temporary outpost here, in the Cove of the Withlacoochee, for a detachment of sick and wounded soldiers early in 1836. Forces led by Osceola attacked the makeshift fort repeatedly in indecisive skirmishes until the main army under General Winfield Scott relieved it. The fort site was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.
heritage.visiting: A reconstructed palisade marks the fort site, and four Seminole Heritage Trail kiosks explain the fort and the Seminole people who lived here; a paved path connects to the Withlacoochee State Trail.

places.notes: Source is Citrus County's tourism listing; floridastateparks.org blocks automated reads. Not in the outdoors slice. The listing gives the park number (352) 726-0317. No alerts. Point re-geocoded to 3100 (Census).

places.name: De Soto National Memorial
places.hours_text: Visitor welcome area daily 9:00am–4:45pm; grounds dawn to dusk; parking lot gates close at 5:00pm; closed New Year's Day, Thanksgiving and Christmas
places.summary: A National Park Service site where the Manatee River meets Tampa Bay that commemorates Hernando de Soto's 1539 landing and expedition. It has a monument, a coastal nature trail and ranger programs.

designations.name: National Memorial (authorized by Congress)
National Register of Historic Places (DeSoto National Memorial)
National Register of Historic Places (Shaw's Point Archeological District)

heritage.story: In May 1539 Hernando de Soto's army of soldiers, hired mercenaries, craftsmen and clergy made landfall in Tampa Bay and met fierce resistance from Indigenous people defending their homelands; the expedition became a four-year, 4,000-mile march across the Southeast. Congress authorized the memorial on March 11, 1948, and it was placed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1966. The National Register inventory notes that historians do not agree this was the actual landing site.

places.name: Judah P. Benjamin Confederate Memorial at Gamble Plantation Historic State Park
places.summary: The tabby mansion of Robert Gamble's sugar plantation on the Manatee River, worked by enslaved people, later donated to the state as a Confederate memorial. It is a state park seen on guided tours.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Benjamin, Judah P., Memorial / Robert Gamble House)

heritage.story: Major Robert Gamble built the mansion between about 1845 and 1850 as the center of a sugar plantation that at its height covered 3,500 acres; he likely enslaved more than 200 people to work the land and process the cane. Its columns and two-foot-thick walls are tabby, a mix used in place of brick. Confederate cabinet officer Judah P. Benjamin stayed there in May 1865 while fleeing Union forces. In 1925 the United Daughters of the Confederacy bought the house and grounds and gave them to the state as a memorial to Benjamin; the mansion was listed in the National Register in 1970, and the state added the ruins of the sugar mill to the park in 2002.
heritage.visiting: The mansion is seen on guided tours, six a day Thursday through Monday; the grounds include a 40,000-gallon cistern and the 1872 Patten House, and the fenced ruins of the sugar mill are half a mile north on State Road 683.

places.quote: This antebellum mansion was home to Major Robert Gamble and is the only surviving plantation house in South Florida.

places.summary: A 10-acre state archaeological site on Terra Ceia Island with a 20-foot flat-topped temple mound built of shell and sand over some 2,000 years of Indigenous occupation.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Madira Bickel Mounds)

heritage.story: Excavations show Indigenous occupation reaching back about 2,000 years across the Manasota, Weedon Island and Safety Harbor cultures, whose people raised a ceremonial mound of shell, sand and village debris about 20 feet high on a base about 100 by 170 feet, with a ramp on its western side. Madira Bickel of Sarasota and her husband Karl bought the land around the mound and donated it to the state in 1948; it was the first Native American site in Florida designated a State Archaeological Site and was listed in the National Register in 1970. The remains of the Prine Burial Mound are also in the park.
heritage.visiting: Stairs lead to a fenced overlook on top of the mound.

The state park estimates that as many as 7,500 Native Americans may have visited it each year to trade and bury their dead. It holds burial mounds, temple or platform mounds, a plaza and a large midden; Citrus County's tourism office says Temple Mound A remains the highest point in Crystal River. places.name: Frank Lloyd Wright Architecture at Florida Southern College
places.address: 840 Johnson Ave (Sharp Family Tourism and Education Center)
places.hours_text: Visitor center daily 9:30 a.m.–4:30 p.m. (closed Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year's Day); Basic Campus Tour daily at 10 a.m. and 2 p.m.; In-Depth Tour daily at 10:30 a.m. and 1 p.m.
places.summary: Thirteen buildings Frank Lloyd Wright designed for Florida Southern College in Lakeland from 1938, which the college calls the largest single-site collection of his architecture. Docent-led walking tours start at the Sharp Family Tourism and Education Center.

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Florida Southern College Architectural District)
National Historic Landmark (Florida Southern College Historic District)

heritage.story: College president Ludd Spivey asked Frank Lloyd Wright to design a new campus in 1938, and Wright first walked the grounds, a citrus-covered hill above Lake Hollingsworth, on May 8, 1938, envisioning buildings growing 'out of the ground and into the light – a Child of the Sun.' Over more than 20 years he delivered 18 designs, and 13 were built, beginning with the Annie Pfeiffer Chapel (1938–1941); students supplied labor for the first five, and during World War II the crew was almost entirely women. The buildings are linked by more than a mile of covered walkways, the Esplanade. The campus was designated a National Historic Landmark in 2012.
heritage.visiting: A 90-minute Basic Campus Tour visits the Pfeiffer Chapel, the E. T. Roux Library and the Usonian Faculty House; a 2.5-hour In-depth Tour adds Danforth Chapel, the Ordway Arts Building and the Polk County Science Building with Wright's only planetarium. Tickets are sold at the GEICO Gift Shop, 840 Johnson Avenue.

places.quote: This easily makes Florida Southern the world’s largest single-site collection of Wright’s architecture for one client, as well as his only executed design for a college campus.

places.summary: Pinellas County's oldest park, 92 acres in Safety Harbor, built around the Tocobaga temple mound of the Safety Harbor Site, a National Historic Landmark.

heritage.story: The park holds the Safety Harbor Site, identified with Tocobaga, the 16th-century capital of the Tocobaga people, and the type site of the Safety Harbor culture. Its temple mound, about 150 feet across and 20 feet high, is built of alternating layers of shell and sand; the county calls it the largest remaining mound in the Tampa Bay region. Spanish explorers described the town as the Tocobaga capital, and the site was probably abandoned by 1700. The county acquired the property in 1948, and the site was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1964.

heritage.story: Tampa architect Willis R. Biggers designed the courthouse, built in 1912, and it was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1992. The historical society says it draws on four architectural styles, two European and two American, and that it sits at a 45-degree angle on the downtown square so each of its four doorways faces a compass point. Today it is the Old Courthouse Heritage Museum, with exhibits on 12,000 years of Citrus County and Florida history.

places.name: Dade Battlefield Historic State Park
places.hours_text: 8 a.m. to sunset, 365 days a year; visitor center 9 a.m.–5 p.m.
places.summary: A state park near Bushnell on the site of Dade's Battle of December 28, 1835, which opened the Second Seminole War. Its visitor center has a small museum on the Seminole wars, and a reenactment of the battle is held each January.
places.quote: Established in 1921 to preserve and commemorate the site of Dade's Battle of 1835, a momentous event that spawned the longest and most costly American Indian war in U.S. history

designations.name: National Register of Historic Places (Dade Battlefield Historic Memorial)
National Historic Landmark

heritage.story: On the morning of December 28, 1835, about 130 Seminoles led by Micanopy, with Black Seminole allies, ambushed Major Francis L. Dade and more than 100 soldiers marching on the Fort King Road to reinforce Fort King, near present-day Ocala; all but three of Dade's soldiers were killed. The battle opened the Second Seminole War, which the state park calls the longest and most costly American Indian war in U.S. history. Florida set the site aside as a memorial park in 1921; it was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1972 and designated a National Historic Landmark in 1973.
heritage.visiting: The visitor center has a small museum with artifacts and exhibits on the Florida Seminole wars and a 12-minute video about the battle. About 2,000 people attend the park's battle reenactment each January, per the park; the grounds have trails through pine flatwoods and oak hammock, picnic pavilions and an indoor lodge.

heritage.story: Pinellas County's Parks & Conservation Resources Department has run Heritage Village as the county's local history museum since 1976, on 21 acres of the Pinewood Cultural Park. Its more than 28 historic structures range from an 1850s log cabin built by Clearwater's founding families, which the museum calls the oldest extant structure in the county, to the 1924 Gandy Tower that marked the entrance to the Gandy Bridge, the first bridge across the bay between St. Petersburg and Tampa, and a 1930s sponge warehouse from Tarpon Springs. The collection holds more than 14,000 objects, and the archives and library more than 9,000 photographs.
heritage.visiting: Walk the paths between the houses, several furnished as period rooms, and visit the two gallery spaces; admission is free.

heritage.story: The city's register lists the Pinellas Point Mound at 1811–1827 Mound Place South as a local historic landmark, designated in March 2003.
